qs.q: A 58-year-old man with unresectable pancreatic cancer undergoes successful percutaneous placement of a self-expanding metal stent across a malignant biliary stricture. What is the primary long-term advantage of a metal stent over a plastic catheter in this setting?
o: Total removal of the need for any future interventions
Prevention of external bile loss and resulting fat malabsorption
Larger diameter yielding longer patency before tumor ingrowth
Reduced rate of immediate post‑procedure bile peritonitis
qs.e: Self-expanding metal stents have a wider caliber, which results in significantly longer patency compared to narrow plastic stents. They do not completely eliminate long-term complications or future interventions.
qs.s: PTC and Percutaneous Biliary Drainage in Obstructive Jaundice: MCQs

qs.q: A patient presents with severe jaundice, dark urine, and pale stools due to an external compression of the bile duct by pancreatic cancer. What type of accumulated bilirubin is primarily responsible for these findings?
qs.e: Post-hepatic or obstructive jaundice results from a blockage in bile flow, leading to an accumulation of conjugated bilirubin. This causes high conjugated bilirubin in serum and urine along with pale stools.

qs.q: Which tumour marker is monitored in pancreatic cancer, although it can also be elevated in benign conditions such as chronic pancreatitis and cholestasis?
qs.e: CA 19-9 is a tumour marker for pancreatic cancer that lacks specificity and can be elevated in cholestasis or chronic pancreatitis. CEA serves as a secondary tumour marker.
qs.s: Clinical Chemical Pathology Crash Course — Part 2: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with advanced pancreatic cancer develops migratory thrombophlebitis, a hypercoagulable state known as Trousseau syndrome. This condition is most characteristically associated with which tumor?
qs.e: Trousseau syndrome, or migratory thrombophlebitis, is associated with tumor hypercoagulability seen in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. Benign lesions like serous cystadenomas do not typically present with systemic paraneoplastic clotting disorders.
qs.s: Pancreatic Disorders: A Comprehensive Review: MCQs

qs.q: Which of the following complications is most directly linked to perineural invasion by pancreatic cancer cells?
o: Hypercoagulable state leading to increased clot formation
Accumulation of ascitic fluid within the abdominal cavity
Back pain radiating from the abdomen caused by nerve invasion
Development of obstructive jaundice due to bile duct blockage
qs.e: Perineural invasion causes neuropathic back pain. The other complications arise from different mechanisms.
qs.s: Pancreatic Disorders: A Comprehensive Review: MCQs

qs.q: Which precursor lesion follows a stepwise progression from low‑grade to high‑grade dysplasia before becoming invasive pancreatic cancer?
o: Acinar cell carcinoma, an aggressive pancreatic cancer type
Pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN) progressing to carcinoma
Serous cystadenoma, a benign cystic pancreatic tumor
Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN) as a precursor lesion
qs.e: PanIN progresses from grades I‑III to invasive carcinoma. IPMN is a separate cystic precursor, while the others are not precursors.
qs.s: Pancreatic Disorders: A Comprehensive Review: MCQs

qs.q: A 30‑year‑old patient with a strong family history of pancreatic cancer tests positive for a germline mutation in which gene?
qs.e: BRCA2 germline mutations are associated with familial pancreatic cancer. KRAS, TP53, and SMAD4 are somatic mutations in sporadic PDAC.
qs.s: Pancreatic Disorders: A Comprehensive Review: MCQs

qs.q: Which clinical syndrome is most closely associated with the hypercoagulable state of pancreatic cancer?
qs.e: Trousseau syndrome describes migratory thrombophlebitis linked to pancreatic malignancy. The other syndromes are unrelated to cancer‑associated coagulopathy.
qs.s: Pancreatic Disorders: A Comprehensive Review: MCQs
